newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: FEATURE - Landsbergis eyes comeback in Lithuania election. [CORRECTED 9:23 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Landsbergis eyes comeback in Lithuania election. [CORRECTED 9:23 GMT]

text.p: Former Lithuanian leader and independence hero Vytautas Landsbergis is bidding for a political comeback in elections this month, riding on popular disillusionment with the current government of former communists, his long-time opponents.
(Corrects to remove reference to Landsbergis being president. He was head of the supreme council -- de facto head of state, but not carrying the title of president).

As Lithuania heads for a general election on October 20, Landsbergis's right-wing Homeland Union party leads the ruling Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP), born from the ashes of the Lithuanian Communist Party, in opinion polls.
"People have lost the enthusiasm we had when we first regained our independence. They have lost confidence in the state," Landsbergis told Reuters.

Four years ago, to the surprise of many, the bearded and bespectacled music professor was defeated at the ballot box despite his role as leader and symbol of Lithuania's drive to independence from the Soviet Union.
The confrontation with Moscow won him and his country much admiration, especially after 13 people were killed in January 1991 in Moscow's backlash against the independence movement.

But Lithuanians, reeling from the economic crisis which followed independence, dumped Landsbergis in 1992 for what they knew best: the ex-communists of the LDLP and reformist leader Algirdas Brazauskas, who became president a year later.
The country's left turn was mirrored elsewhere in eastern Europe, where ex-communists have been propelled back to power.

Analysts say Landsbergis's party is likely to ally with the Christian Democrats to form the next government, although they may be forced to invite in other parties if they fall short of a majority in the 141-seat parliament.

In the latest opinion poll by Baltic Research for the newspaper Respublika, the Homeland Union had the support of 14.7 percent of decided voters, the LDLP 12 percent, the populist Centre Party 10.5 percent and the Christian Democrats 9.3 percent.
But uncertainty still ruled as about a quarter of those polled, and who intended to vote, had not decided who to vote for.

The next prime minister is expected to be Gediminas Vagnorius, a close ally of Landsbergis who was premier between January 1991 and July 1992 and oversaw the dismantling of the collective farm system.
Landsbergis himself is expected to become parliamentary speaker and prepare for a 1998 presidential battle against Brazauskas.

In an electoral battle full of strong personalities, another former prime minister, Kazimiera Prunskiene, sacked in early 1991 and later accused of working for the feared KGB Soviet security police, will lead her Womens' Party into the fray.
"The restoration and rebuilding of Lithuania was our work," Landsbergis said. "It is painful to see your work damaged. We hope to repair the damage done by the current government."
The LDLP is suffering from a backlash because it failed to fulfil populist promises made when it was swept to power.
Instead of making life easier, it followed an austerity programme recommended by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

It has also been discredited by a banking crisis, in which a former prime minister withdrew his cash from a leading bank days before it was shut by the authorities, increasing widespread popular cynicism and belief in government corruption.

"People, especially farmers, the poor and pensioners, pinned a lot of hope on the LDLP and they have been disappointed," said Arturas Racas, a political journalist and commentator with the leading daily Lietuvos Rytas.
Lithuania has been congratulated by the IMF for its reform policies and has been accepted by the international banking community as a partner with which it can do business.

But macroeconomic gains, likely to lead to growth of between one and two percent this year and which have seen inflation fall from 1,200 percent a month to 23.9 percent in August, are hardly reflected in people's daily lives.
Prices for heating are rising, although not by as much as the IMF would like, pensioners live on a pittance of an average $46 month and the average wage is just $168 a month.
The 1996 U.N. Human Development Report for Lithuania said real urban incomes at the end of 1995 were 40 percent of their December 1990 level while rural incomes were 29 percent.
Much LDLP support in 1992 came from the countryside, where a third of the population lives and which was then suffering from the impact of decollectivisation.
But the LDLP did little to improve the farmers' lot and many still use horse-drawn ploughs on tiny, unviable plots of land.
Diplomats say Landsbergis's party may have to back down from its populist pledges of tax cuts, pension and public sector pay rises, which it says will be funded by better tax collection.

Foreign policy is not expected to change much, with the emphasis on NATO and European Union (EU) entry, although some analysts worry the Homeland Union's confrontational style and well-aired mistrust of Russia will lead to tenser relations.
